title: Dorothy Becomes an Early Adopter.
subtitle: Chapter 4, in my Wizard of Oz parody
body_html:
The Wizard of Oz is a timeless classic. I have ruined it, to explain health insurance.

“A Word From Our Sponsors…”

If you are looking for mental healthcare, join us at Radial—where your author works. We focus on next-generation treatments—beyond “just meds.”

These treatments include Spravato, Nightware, eTNS, PRISM Neurofeedback, and soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief, TMS, Accelerated TMS, and fMRI-guided SAINT TMS.

Get Care At Radial

Dorothy awoke to an email in her inbox.  Her searching the night before had led to an invitation!  The email waiting for her was from the founder of a telehealth company.  It said they were looking to interview patients for their advisory board.  “InFlames,” the company was called.  It was…it said a…BaaS company?  Biologics as a Service1.  Dorothy booked a time with the founder for a discovery call later that day.

On a zoom call, Dorothy looked earnestly into the Founder's ring-light-illuminated face.  She was surprised to see one of his eyes slowly wink at her. She thought she must have been mistaken at first, for none of the Founders in Kansas2 ever wink, but presently, the figure nodded its head to her in a friendly way. Maybe it was different with those who were funded in Silicon Valley.

"Good day," said the Founder in a rather husky voice.

"Did you have a question about my experience with psoriasis3?" asked the girl in wonder.

"Certainly," answered the Founder. "How do you do?4"

"I'm pretty well, thank you," replied Dorothy politely. "How do you do?"

"I'm not feeling well," said the Founder, smiling, "for it is very tedious being perched up here night and day trying to scare up traction in a crowded market."

“Can't you raise funds for pay-per-click advertising?" asked Dorothy.

"No, not in this market, and my angel investor has stuck up my @%$. If you will please sign up for our platform solution for patients with mental health and inflammation, that will be traction, and I can probably raise on that,” said the Founder.

Dorothy reached up both thumbs and clicked the subscribe button on her phone, for, being envisioned as a Direct to Consumer play, their app was quite easy to navigate.

"Thank you very much," said the Founder when he had signed up a new subscriber. "I feel like a new man."

Dorothy was puzzled at this, for it sounded odd to hear a Venture-backed HealthTech Founder speak as if one customer like her was a big deal.

"Who are you?" asked the Founder when he had stretched himself and yawned. "And where are you going?"

"My name is Dorothy," said the girl, "I am going to the Crimson City for a Consult with the Specialist.  I’d really like to get the medicine I need, but that requires prior authorization, and apparently, that's pretty tricky. 

"Where is Crimson City?" the Founder inquired, thinking this an important discovery call. "And who is the Specialist?"

"Why don't you know?" she returned in surprise.

"No, indeed. I don't know anything. But, you see, I am stuffed with seed capital.   I raised 5 million for InFlames, just with a pitch deck, so I have no traction," he answered sadly.

"Oh," said Dorothy, "I'm awfully sorry for you.  I guess it’s good that I signed up for your platform."

"Do you think," he asked, "if I go to the Crimson City with you, the Specialist will give me some referrals?   Or maybe even find Product-Market-Fit5?"

"I cannot tell," she returned, "but you may come with me if you like. If the Specialist does not give you any referrals to generate traction, you will be no worse off than you are now6."

"That is true," said the Founder. "You see," he continued confidentially, "I don't mind my bank account being stuffed because I don’t have to raise again in this market. So if anyone shitposts my company, it doesn't matter, for I can't feel it. But I do not want people to call me a fool, and if my bank account stays stuffed with cash, and I don’t execute a Go-To-Market Motion like I did signing up you for the platform, how am I ever going to scale?"

"I understand how you feel," said the little girl, who was genuinely sorry for him. "If you come with me, I'll ask The Specialist to do all he can for you."

"Thank you," he answered gratefully.  “Wow, I just looked.  I live right next door to you!  Our company decided to be all-remote, so I moved to Kansas City, too, to reduce our burn rate!  Maybe we can get some steps together on the way,” asked the Founder.

“I think I should enjoy that very much.  But we need to follow the yellow dotted line on the Patient Journey handout,” said Dorothy.

“Those things are a design nightmare,” said the Founder.

1

For those not in the know, Biologics are a class of drugs frequently utilized in rheumatology, but more and more broadly. Getting to product-market fit with a rheumatology startup isn't something I've seen in the market, but here's an illustration of how the reimbursement model works, at least in theory, for a company of the kind I’m imaging InFlames is:

Doctors work for hospitals or in private practices.  Doctors legally can't own hospitals.  Thirty-five states include prohibitions on non-physicians owning medical practices.  The American medical association, a giant lobbying organization, makes enormous money by owning the Copyright on the billing and coding rubric Current Procedural Terminology.  These CPT codes, a product owned by the AMA, back solve to “relative value units.”   Relative Value Units estimate how much physician time goes into any medical procedure.

CPT codes are brand-named versions of “physician time” accounted for with RVUs.   Let's provide a simple example that doesn't infringe upon anybody's trademark:  It took me 12 minutes to write the above.  Let's assume that one hour of my time is worth one hour of my time, an OVU ( Owen Value Unit).   The beginning of this chapter would be worth 0.2 OVUs.   But the American Medical Association has decided that “Chapter Writing” needs a code associated with it.  I will make up right now so I don't get sued:   Let’s call it 55505 in our Current Writing Terminology system (so it’s a CWT code).  This code would be associated with a diagnosis.  Diagnosis codes are all from an international set which the AMA didn't also trademark.  International classification of disease, 10th Edition, is our current standard (ICD-10), Like F80.1 (Expressive Language Disorder…What we used to call dyslexia).  So for a dyslexic writer, like your author, the above would be submitted if writing this book was paid for by Publisher’s Insurance, with the following:

Place of Writing: Office

Tax ID of Writer: (ss#)

Date of Writing: 02/14/2023

CWT: 55505

Associated Dx: F80.1 

This would, of course, have a billed amount.  It was 0.2 OVUs, and my time was $1000/hr.  So I’ll submit a bill to the Publisher’s Insurance company for the total charge for writing that…$200.

Simple, right?

Well, it should be. And in a world without bizarrely incentivized intermediaries, it would be.  Unfortunately, this is not our world.  

The CWT codes remain the same. But now, let's assume that the publisher’s industry is a cartel, which is practically true.   And instead of paying writers for their time, which I illustrated above, they take out insurance on the payments they'll have to provide to writers.   So they will pay somebody else to manage the risk that I will write something too long.   You will also, at some point, notice that there's no incentive in the above system for me to write anything specific.   I could've just written all work, and no play makes jack a dull boy over and over again, but if it took me 12 minutes, that would be 0.2 OVUs; I'm giving my dyslexia, they can't expect much better, so I submit the same bill all over again.

I bet you see the problem already.   It doesn't make a lot of sense to pay people to write. It doesn't make much sense to take out insurance because people might write the wrong thing, write too much, or write too little.   So paying someone to write and not caring what they write about is not a system that has existed historically because it's completely Nonsensical.  And then using an insurance market to make those payments and inserting a bunch of Intermediaries, platform solutions, kickbacks, legalized kickbacks, regulatory compliance… It would be exactly as compelling as Twitter is on average.  

A fee-for-service healthcare system already doesn't work well. Some people are going to get very sick.  These people will require a lot of health care. Almost axiomatically, the very sick can’t pay for things that are very expensive and complicated.  It's not fair to make them. It's not reasonable to expect them to do so. At a bare minimum, babies in the neonatal intensive care unit don't have a day job. So that cost alone has to get spread out.  I am a libertarian, for the most part.  But that social contract around who wins and who loses financially doesn't work when it is the most vulnerable who lose.  It's morally unacceptable.  It's financially devastating.  And it reduces the risk-taking necessary for a dynamic economy if we all manage because anybody we know could get wholly ruined.  Oops, that's what's happening now!

So we have to do something to manage the risk that rare, very bad things could happen to people that nobody can afford, nor should they have to.  Everyone sleeps better at night if this is the case.  Insurance is usually how we manage the risk that is rare and expensive.  The issue, of course, is that when you create a system where people have an incentive to act riskier because they won't have to pay for it, you get what we call a moral hazard.  Let me illustrate that concept:

Let's imagine a world with readers’ insurance.  In that world, readers’ insurance will function as health insurance does now.  Instead of indemnifying you against the catastrophically lousy book, which is rare, let's use that insurance policy to pay for every book you buy.  We have now created a problem.  You no longer have an incentive to be picky about the books you purchase.  It makes sense to buy every book; it's on the insurance company's tab!  Now, you're buying books to ensure you get your money’s worth out of your readers’ insurance.  Voracious readers will opt-in.  Their decision-making around which books to obtain will become significantly less rigorous. People who don't like to read at all won’t want to be bothered by the insurance.  If you imagined that books could cost $1 million each, you wouldn't even get to see the price before you bought it, and he wouldn't care because your insurance theoretically paid, you get the idea.  Insurance isn't a great way to handle most markets.  I will point out that we don't have an insurance system in America in any meaningful sense. We have a brutal mashup between a protection racket and Shirley Jackson's 1948 classic “The Lottery.”

Since the 1940s, healthcare has gotten wildly more complex and more expensive in both its delivery and payment models.   Insurance markets work well when you can predict what the expense will be.   Actuarial math isn't that complicated.  If ten people are going to cost $1000, and there are 10,000 of them, the total cost is $10,000 a year, and any insurance policy beyond one dollar per person per year will be profitable!

2

I would be remiss if I did not provide a shout-out to my Kansas colleagues building technology companies. Especially TripleBlind! Damn, that is a good idea:

TripleBlind drives data collaboration by automatically de-identifying data. Deliver collaborative analytics and model training to your partners — by never moving, sharing, or storing raw data.

Global healthcare providers can accelerate research, reduce costs, generate new business opportunities, and minimize the liabilities of transferring protected health information (PHI).

With General Catalyst as a Funder too!

3

Given the inflammatory nature of both, there is emerging evidence of the link between psoriasis and psychiatric conditions.*

Psoriasis is linked with many mental disorders…Chronic stress diminishes the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and upregulates sympathetic-adrenal-medullary responses, stimulating pro-inflammatory cytokines. Then, it maintains and exacerbates psoriasis and some of its mental disorders. High levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines connect psoriasis, psychiatric conditions, and other comorbidities of psoriasis (such as atherosclerosis) within a vicious cycle. Furthermore, the etiopathogenesis of the link between each psychiatric comorbidity and psoriasis has its own subtleties, including the cooccurrence of other comorbidities, the parts of the body affected by psoriasis, treatments, and biological and psychosocial factors.

*Ferreira BI, Abreu JL, Reis JP, Figueiredo AM. Psoriasis and Associated Psychiatric Disorders: A Systematic Review on Etiopathogenesis and Clinical Correlation. J Clin Aesthet Dermatol. 2016 Jun;9(6):36-43. Epub 2016 Jun 1. PMID: 27386050; PMCID: PMC4928455.

4

It’s worth highlighting this kind of curious open-ended questioning is excellent!

5

In fairness, finding a product-market fit in healthcare is extremely difficult. However, recently, a16z bio published a great piece on market annealing, which should be mandatory reading for those in health care and healthcare. Thanks, Martin Casado!

6

The brilliant Curtis LeMay, the Air Force General, had a saying: “I don't have time to distinguish between the unfortunate and the incompetent.” He had a bias toward doing something when something needed to be done. Even when it wasn't clear with the right thing was.
